title: Second Reading of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill
what_it_is: A Bill at Second Reading, moved by the Second Minister for Home Affairs on behalf of the Senior Minister, amending the Road Traffic Act to strengthen penalties for dangerous driving, tighten alcohol limits, create a drug-driving offence, and enhance enforcement.
why_it_matters: The Bill creates a new offence of purposeful endangerment carrying up to 15 years' imprisonment and lifetime disqualification, lowers the prescribed alcohol limits, makes holding a mobile phone while a vehicle is in motion an offence, and introduces a presence-based drug-driving offence. It also allows automated notices for traffic offences and tightens the Driver Improvement Points System from January 2027.

key_points.point: The Second Minister moved that the Bill be read a Second time.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: That the Bill be now read a Second time.

key_points.point: The Bill has three objectives: strengthen accountability for the most egregious road conduct, further deter driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and enhance the Traffic Police's ability to detect and enforce against traffic offences.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: to achieve three key objectives: First, strengthen accountability for the most egregious road conduct; Second, further deter driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs; and third, enhance the Traffic Police's ability to detect and enforce against traffic offences.

key_points.point: Clause 6 introduces a new offence of purposeful endangerment.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Clause 6, therefore, introduces a new offence of purposeful endangerment.

key_points.point: Where death is caused under the purposeful endangerment offence, the offender may be imprisoned up to 15 years and is liable to fine or caning, or both.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Where death is caused, the offender is to be punished with imprisonment, which may extend to 15 years and is also liable to fine or caning, or both.

key_points.point: The Court must impose lifetime driving disqualification for purposeful endangerment unless there are special reasons, in which case at least 10 years' disqualification applies.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: The Court must also impose driving disqualification for life, unless there are special reasons not to do so; and if special reasons apply, the Court must impose at least 10 years of driving disqualification.

key_points.point: The Bill increases the maximum imprisonment for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt from five to seven years for first-time offenders and from 10 to 13 years for repeat offenders.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: the Bill increases the maximum imprisonment term for first-time offenders from five years to seven years, and for repeat offenders from 10 years to 13 years.

key_points.point: The maximum additional imprisonment uplift for serious offenders increases from one year to one and a half years.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: the maximum uplift for serious offenders will increase from one year to one and a half years' imprisonment.

key_points.point: The Bill tightens prescribed alcohol limits from exceeding 35 microgrammes to 15 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath, and from exceeding 80 milligrammes to 30 milligrammes per 100 millilitres of blood.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: tighten the prescribed alcohol limits from exceeding 35 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath, to 15 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath; and from exceeding 80 milligrammes of alcohol per 100 millilitres of blood, to 30 milligrammes of alcohol per 100 millilitres of blood.

key_points.point: Clause 11 introduces a new offence of driving or attempting to drive with a specified substance present in blood, without separately proving impairment.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Clause 11 therefore introduces a new offence under the new section 67(1)(c) of the RTA, where a person who drives or attempts to drive with the presence of a specified substance in his blood will commit an offence, without separately proving that he was impaired whilst driving.

key_points.point: A statutory defence applies where the substance was lawfully consumed or administered and the person did not know or have reason to believe it could impair driving.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: The Bill provides a statutory defence where the substance was lawfully consumed by or administered; and the person did not know or have reason to believe that consuming it could impair his or her driving.

key_points.point: Clause 14 removes the requirement to administer a preliminary breath test, streamlining drink-driving enforcement.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: clause 14 of the Bill removes the requirement to administer a preliminary breath test, streamlining the drink-driving enforcement process.

key_points.point: Clause 16 removes the authorisation requirement for taking blood specimens from hospital patients under the RTA, aligning it with the Criminal Procedure Code.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Clause 16 therefore removes the authorisation requirement under the RTA, aligning it with the Criminal Procedure Code provisions.

key_points.point: Clause 10 amends section 65B so that holding a mobile communication device while the vehicle is in motion is an offence, without needing to prove the driver was operating it.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Clause 10 therefore amends section 65B to remove the element stating that the driver must be operating the device. A driver who holds a mobile communication device in his hand while the vehicle is in motion will commit an offence.

key_points.point: Touching a device secured in a mount while driving is not an offence.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: This amendment also makes clear that it is not an offence if the device is secured in a mount and a driver touches it while driving.

key_points.point: Clause 21 introduces section 81A, allowing a computer program to assess evidence and automatically issue a notice requiring the vehicle owner to provide the driver's particulars.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Clause 21 introduces a new section 81A, which allows a computer program to assess whether there is sufficient evidence that a traffic offence was committed and if so, automatically issue a notice to require the vehicle owner to provide the particulars of the driver at the time of the alleged offence.

key_points.point: The Bill amends provisions to make clear how driving disqualification periods are calculated.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: First, the Bill amends a number of provisions in the RTA to make clear how driving disqualification periods are calculated.

key_points.point: The Driver Improvement Points System will be tightened from January 2027, lowering the suspension threshold from 24 to 18 demerit points and lengthening suspension periods.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: we announced last week that we will tighten the Driver Improvement Points System, commonly known as the demerit points regime, to be implemented from January 2027. The two key changes are the lowering of the suspension threshold from 24 demerit points to 18 and lengthening the suspension periods for errant drivers who meet this lowered threshold.

key_points.point: Mr Vikram Nair asked whether the new purposeful endangerment offence is necessary given existing Penal Code offences.
key_points.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
key_points.quote: My question is whether this is necessary as I believe such a person can probably be prosecuted under existing offences where such a person can be charged for intending to cause death or grievous hurt under the Penal Code.

key_points.point: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong supported the introduction of penalties for purposeful endangerment, tightened alcohol limits, the standalone drug driving framework, and automated enforcement.
key_points.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
key_points.quote: I fully support the introduction of penalties for purposeful endangerment, the tightening of legal alcohol limits, the standalone drug driving framework and the transition towards automated enforcement technology.

key_points.point: Dr Wan Rizal asked the Ministry to commit to a review in a few years.
key_points.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
key_points.quote: I would ask the Ministry to commit to a review in a few years.

key_points.point: Ms He Ting Ru noted that the Bill does not raise the corresponding fines for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.
key_points.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
key_points.quote: It does not raise the corresponding fines.

key_points.point: Dr Hamid Razak asked for safeguards to ensure suspension powers remain proportionate, transparent and timely.
key_points.speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
key_points.quote: Could the Minister therefore elaborate on the safeguards that will ensure that these suspension powers remain proportionate, transparent and timely?

key_points.point: Mr Andre Low asked the Minister to explain the evidence supporting the precise alcohol limits of 15 microgrammes and 30 milligrammes.
key_points.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
key_points.quote: I ask the Minister to explain the evidence supporting the precise limits of 15 microgrammes and 30 milligrammes that we have chosen

key_points.point: Ms Mariam Jaafar supported the new offence of purposeful endangerment and increased penalties for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.
key_points.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
key_points.quote: I fully support the Bill's central changes, including the new offence of purposeful endangerment and the increased penalties for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.

key_points.point: Mr David Hoe supported the change to the mobile phone offence because holding a device may already distract a driver.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
key_points.quote: I support this change because the driver holding a phone or another communication device may already be distracted even if it is difficult to prove whether he or she was typing, making a call or using a particular mobile app.

key_points.point: Mr Yip Hon Weng supported the Bill, saying it strengthens deterrence, modernises enforcement and closes gaps.
key_points.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
key_points.quote: I support this Bill. It strengthens deterrence, modernises enforcement and closes gaps.

key_points.point: The Minister said that where facts satisfy more than one offence provision, the Attorney-General's Chambers will exercise prosecutorial discretion to determine the appropriate offence.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: If the facts and circumstances of a case can satisfy more than one offence provision, whether in the same Act or across different Acts, the Attorney-General's Chambers will exercise its prosecutorial discretion to determine the appropriate offence to prefer.

key_points.point: The Minister said what constitutes special reasons for departing from lifetime disqualification is ultimately for the Courts to decide.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: What constitutes "special reasons" in the context of purposeful endangerment is ultimately to be decided by the Courts.

key_points.point: The Minister said forfeiture of a vehicle not belonging to the offender will not be ordered if the offender used it without the owner's consent.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: the Court is to make an order for the forfeiture of the motor vehicle unless the Court is satisfied that the person who has committed the offence is not the owner of the motor vehicle and the person who has committed the offence had used the motor vehicle without the owner's consent.

key_points.point: The Minister said the Bill focused on imprisonment terms for egregious driving offences and did not review fines.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: we have focused on addressing these egregious forms of driving and therefore, have only reviewed the imprisonment terms for these offences.

key_points.point: The Minister said the new drug presence offence does not apply to most common medicines or over-the-counter medicines.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: the new offence does not apply to most common medicines or over-the-counter medicines.

key_points.point: The Minister said the laboratory applies validated analytical limits and reporting criteria for specified substances in blood.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: The laboratory applies validated analytical limits and reporting criteria when reporting the presence of specified substances in blood.

key_points.point: The Minister said the Traffic Police and Home Team Science and Technology Agency will ensure Handheld Breath Evidential Analyser models meet evidential grade standards.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: The Traffic Police, with the support of the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, will ensure that the deployed Handheld Breath Evidential Analyser models meet evidential grade standards through testing and certifications

key_points.point: The Minister said there is no reason to provide breath-testing devices for drivers to self-check alcohol levels.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: There is thus no reason to provide breath-testing devices in the market for drivers to self-check their alcohol levels.

key_points.point: The Minister said the amendment makes enforcement easier as the Traffic Police will no longer need to prove the driver was operating the device.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: The amendment will make enforcement easier, as the Traffic Police will no longer need to prove that the driver was operating the device for the offence to be made out.

key_points.point: The Minister said the use of a mounted device while a vehicle is in motion has not been criminalised because there are legitimate reasons such as navigation.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: We have not criminalised the use of a mounted device while a vehicle is in motion, as we appreciate that there are legitimate reasons to do so, such as using navigation applications.

key_points.point: The Minister said it is not an offence for drivers to drive with wearable devices worn in the manner intended by the manufacturer.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Under the current section 65B(1A) of the Road Traffic Act, it is not an offence for drivers to drive with wearable devices worn in the manner intended by the manufacturer of the device.

key_points.point: The Minister said automated notices will only be sent for technical traffic offences prescribed in subsidiary legislation.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: automated notices will only be sent for technical traffic offences, which will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

key_points.point: The Minister said most appeals are dealt with within a month, though complex appeals can take up to three months.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: Most appeals are dealt with within a month, though more complex appeals can take up to three months to process.

key_points.point: The Minister said a one-time deduction of demerit points will apply across the board from 1 January 2027 as a transitionary measure.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: we think it is better to apply the same one-time deduction of demerit points across the board come 1 January 2027 as a transitionary measure

key_points.point: The Minister said the amendments are planned to be operationalised in early 2027.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: ahead of the planned operationalisation of the amendments in early 2027.

key_points.point: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat asked whether section 63A is intended to apply to vehicular ramming attacks and attempted suicide by vehicle.
key_points.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
key_points.quote: I would like to clarify whether it is the legislative intent of section 63A to apply to vehicular ramming attacks and the attempted suicide by vehicle, which were the two scenarios I mentioned.

key_points.point: The Minister replied that it depends on the facts and circumstances of each case, and that such conduct could also be liable under existing offences in other laws.
key_points.speaker: Ms Sim Ann
key_points.quote: It depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. But on their own, currently, they could also be liable for existing offences in other laws.

not_said: Will the Bill be passed at Second Reading?
What is the exact commencement date of the amendments?
How will the new drug presence offence apply to workers exposed to intoxicating substances in the course of work?
Will fines for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt be raised?
What accuracy and validation standards must the automated enforcement computer program meet before deployment?
Will a Vision Zero target for road safety be adopted?
How will the new rules be communicated to platform workers and vocational drivers before enforcement begins?
Will a differentiated demerit points regime for vocational drivers be introduced?
